content: Since 2009, sites 5–6 and 11–19 have been integrated into the network with support from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF) project. Effective pesticide life-cycle management requires a multisectoral approach at both national and international levels. The project has successfully established national steering committees in participating countries, involving sectors such as health, agriculture, and the environment. These committees oversee situation analyses, needs assessments, and the development and implementation of national action plans. This achievement should be promoted across all Member States. Such collaboration is essential to optimize the use of limited resources in countries. The multisectoral approach, along with international collaboration and information exchange during the project’s implementation, has strengthened partnerships between the World Health Organization (WHO) and United Nations organizations, particularly the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). This collaboration has been instrumental in providing harmonized, coordinated, and complementary guidance to national programs and stakeholders for sound pesticide management. The development of joint guidance documents, norms on pesticide management, social mobilization, and increased political support are key outcomes of this collaboration. Additionally, engagement with the pesticide industry as a critical stakeholder in public health pesticide management has been significantly enhanced. This project represents the first global investment dedicated to improving public health pesticide management. It has laid a strong foundation for future strategies and actions to enhance the sound management of these chemicals. Strengthened collaboration with United Nations organizations, industry, and research institutions has led to the development of authoritative guidelines, standards, and norms for pesticide management. The establishment of National Steering Committees in participating countries has facilitated joint situation analyses, needs assessments, and the development of national action plans, with reasonable success in mobilizing additional resources in some countries. However, resource mobilization remains a significant challenge in others. The project’s outcomes and lessons learned have been disseminated through peer-reviewed journals, WHO publications, and WHO-organized meetings. This has raised awareness among policymakers and program managers, leading to actions for sound pesticide management. Evidence of this includes the development of regional frameworks for pesticide management in WHO’s Western Pacific and Eastern Mediterranean regions, as well as a regional resolution in the Eastern Mediterranean Region. The findings have also been shared with relevant WHO advisory committees to guide priority actions and future activities. Despite these achievements, weak pesticide legislation and national policies, particularly in the health sector, remain the greatest challenges. To address this, WHO, in collaboration with FAO and the United Nations Environment Programme, has revised the International Code of Conduct on the Distribution and Use of Pesticides and developed FAO/WHO guidelines on pesticide legislation. Guidance documents on national pesticide management policies have also been published. Member States are urged to establish or strengthen their national capacity to regulate pesticides throughout their life cycle. Future investments in public health pesticide management should build on the evidence generated by this project, prioritizing the development of comprehensive pesticide policies and legislation. This includes integrating pesticide management into national health policies, developing legislation covering all stages of the pesticide life cycle, establishing mechanisms for intersectoral cooperation, and allocating sufficient resources for effective implementation. Public health pesticide management remains a neglected area with insufficient resources. The WHO Pesticide Evaluation Scheme (WHOPES) network consists of WHO Collaborating Centres, partner institutions, and field sites. Each institution has designated tasks and has benefited from recent capacity-building efforts supported by the BMGF project. These institutions include: 1. The International Pesticide Application Research Centre in the UK, focusing on testing insecticide application equipment globally. 2. The Laboratoire de Lutte Contre les Insectes Nuisibles in France, evaluating new public health pesticides and supporting site assessments and training. 3. The Vector Control Research Centre in India, conducting research and training on lymphatic filariasis and integrated vector control methods. 4. The Walloon Agricultural Research Centre in Belgium, specializing in pesticide quality control. 5. The Insecticide and Insecticide Resistance Laboratory in India, conducting laboratory testing and evaluation of public health pesticides. 6. The Department of Vector Biology and Control in China, focusing on vector surveillance and management. 7. The Institute of Tropical Medicine in Belgium, conducting field studies on vector control products in collaboration with institutions in Vietnam and Cambodia. 8. The London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine in the UK, conducting field studies in collaboration with institutions in Tanzania. 9. The Institut de Recherche pour le Développement in Benin, conducting field studies on vector control products in West Africa. 10. The Vector Control Research Unit in Malaysia, producing standard tools for laboratory studies on insecticide susceptibility. 11. The Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research in Ghana, conducting field studies on vector control products. 12. The University of the Witwatersrand in South Africa, conducting field studies on vector control products. 13. The Medical Research Council in The Gambia, conducting field studies on vector control products. 14. The Manatee County Mosquito Control in the USA, conducting field studies on vector control products. 15. The Regional Medical Research Centre in India, conducting field studies on vector control products. 16. The Kenya Medical Research Institute in Kenya, conducting field studies on vector control products. 17. The Centre for Disease Control in China, conducting field studies on vector control products. 18. The Instituto Nacional de Salud Pública in Mexico, conducting field studies on vector control products. 19. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in the USA, conducting field studies and quality control of pesticides. These institutions have received support for site assessments, training, equipment provision, and the development of standard protocols for laboratory and field studies.
